name: Omar Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. Could you start by telling me a little about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Omar, 27. I'm a nurse on a general surgical ward at St Columba's Hospital, about a year and a half qualified, with a two-year diploma. I live on my own in a rented flat near Market Road. I lived with my parents for years and saved, and my brother Kerem and I bought a small flat together that we rent out, so I'm all right for money.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal working day look like for you? What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Day shifts, half seven to eight. It's people after operations: checking wounds and drains, pain relief, getting them up and walking the next morning even when they don't want to. I like it when the bay runs smoothly and everyone's comfortable by lunchtime. What wears me out is the complicated dressings, because I'm still slow at them, and the computer, which I avoid as much as I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: it's a computer, not a nurse. At work I'd probably just shrug, because most of us never had time to use it anyway. I don't post online much, maybe a joke in the five-a-side football group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be glad. I write my notes in my little notebook first and type them up after, which drives my ward manager mad, but it's how I keep track. If nothing big changes, I don't have to change either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new. I'd keep doing my day shifts on the surgical ward, keep my notebook, and do my mandatory training when it's due. The rent from the flat with Kerem keeps coming in, and I'd keep saving like I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the notebook drives your manager mad. Why keep it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the hospital computer system crashed for six hours last spring, I was the only nurse on the bay who knew when everybody's last painkillers were. A notebook doesn't need charging. My manager Sinead still teased me, but she borrowed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your job or money that worries you, even with nothing changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. There are surgical wards at three hospitals within a bus ride, and they're all short of nurses. My worry is more that I'm still slow at the complicated dressings, and the senior nurses notice.

say: I'd say AI was always **a computer**, not a nurse.
I'd make a **joke** in the five-a-side group rather than post anything serious.
think: I'd be **glad**, because I like doing my notes on paper first.
If nothing big changes, I **don't have to change** either.
do: Keep working **day shifts** on the surgical ward with my notebook.
Keep saving and collecting **rent** from the flat I own with Kerem.
S0.quote: When the hospital computer system crashed for six hours last spring, I was the only nurse on the bay who knew when everybody's last painkillers were.
fieldNote: His **paper notebook** is a point of pride since it saved the bay during an outage.
He has **rental income** with his brother on top of his savings.
His real worry is **skill**, being slow at complex dressings, not losing work.

steps.text: Keep working surgical ward day shifts with a paper notebook
Keep saving and collecting rent from the flat co-owned with his brother

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, let the computer write the discharge letters, I never liked them anyway. At work I'd probably moan about having to learn another login. Online, nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't think it touches me much. My day is drains, dressings, getting people out of bed after an operation and keeping an eye on them. The thinking AI takes the letters and the planning, and I was never the one doing the planning anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the training because I'd have to, and I'd use the new system as little as I can get away with. I'd still keep my notebook. And I'd ask to do the complex wound care course, because that's hands-on and nobody's replacing that soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit irritated, like when they change the shift pattern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd use it as little as you can. What if the ward starts measuring who uses it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd use it enough to pass. Like the hand-washing audits: you know what they check, you make sure that's done. I'm not going to fight it, I'm just not going to love it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our ward clerk Barbara books the beds, sends the letters and chases the scans, and she's got two years until she can retire. If a computer does all that, I don't know what they'd keep her for.

say: I'd say the computer can **have the discharge letters**; I never liked them.
I'd **moan** at work about learning another login.
think: My day is **drains and dressings**, which thinking AI barely touches.
AI takes the **planning**, and I was never the one doing it.
do: Do the **required training** and use the system just enough to pass checks.
Ask for the **complex wound care** course, which is hands-on.
Keep my **paper notebook** alongside the new system.
feel: **Calm**, with mild **irritation**, like a changed shift pattern.
S1.quote: Our ward clerk Barbara books the beds, sends the letters and chases the scans, and she's got two years until she can retire.
fieldNote: He sees his work as **hands-on**, so thinking AI feels like someone else's problem.
He'll **comply, not embrace**: enough use to pass any audit.
His concern goes to **Barbara**, the ward clerk two years from retirement.

steps.text: Use the new charting system just enough to pass ward audits
Sign up for the complex wound care course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad, two years, and nobody's ready. At work I'd say the managers had better have a plan, because I don't. Online I'd probably still say nothing, but I'd read everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's 2031 that gets me. By then there are robots that can get a man out of bed after a hip operation and change his dressing, and I'm a nurse who's still learning those exact things. I'd be thirty-two, never used any AI, and the hospital would want people who can run the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the thing I hate and start learning how to use the AI tools, maybe with Kerem, who uses them for his work. I'd stop saving for the car I was going to buy and keep the money in the bank. And I'd look at jobs the robots will take longest to reach, like the mental health wards, where it's all talking and trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because I've got the savings and the rent, but I'd feel like the last man still using a paper map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stop the car. What car?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A second-hand estate, so I can get to my parents' place at weekends without two buses. I've had the money ready for months. In this picture it stays in the bank, and I keep taking the buses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you never use AI. What would be the first thing you'd try?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably asking it to explain a drug I don't know, instead of the big book in the office. Kerem says it's like texting a clever friend. I'd feel stupid with AI at first, but feeling stupid for a month beats being out of a job.

say: I'd say **two years** is mad and nobody is ready.
I'd tell managers they'd **better have a plan**, because I don't.
think: **2031** scares me, when robots can lift and dress patients after surgery.
At thirty-two, with **no AI experience**, I'd look out of date.
do: Start learning **AI tools** with my brother Kerem's help in the first year.
Keep the **car money** in the bank and keep taking buses.
Look at **mental health wards**, where the work is talking and trust.
feel: **Anxious**, like the last man still using a paper map.
Not panicked, thanks to **savings and rent**.
S2.quote: I'd feel stupid with AI at first, but feeling stupid for a month beats being out of a job.
fieldNote: Fast AGI pushes him to **break his own rule** and try AI.
He sees robots in 2031 doing **exactly the tasks** he is still learning.
The **mental health ward** idea shows a practical search for safer ground.
The **postponed car** is a small, concrete sign of his caution.

steps.text: Learn to use AI tools for drug questions with his brother's help
Postpone buying the second-hand estate car and keep taking buses
Look into moving to a mental health ward

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is better, but people will waste three of them arguing. I'd tell the lads at football to start learning something now. At work I'd say it to the other juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is enough for someone like me if I don't bury my head. The notes and letters go in 2031, which I don't mind, and the robots come a few years later, when I'd be thirty-five with eight years in. By 2034 I want to be the nurse who's good at the bits robots are bad at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a course in mental health nursing over the next couple of years, part-time, alongside my surgical shifts. I'd learn the AI tools slowly, one at a time, maybe a year in. And I'd buy the car, because five years is long enough that I'm not going to live on buses for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a hospital inspection that's coming next year, not next week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy the car here but not in the two-year picture. Why the difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with two years I'd want every penny ready. With five, I've got time to earn it back, and the rent from the flat keeps coming. It's a few thousand, not a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say about you moving towards mental health nursing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would ask why I'd leave surgery when surgery sounds important. My mum would understand, because she watched my grandad go downhill with dementia. I'd tell them it's still nursing, just a part the robots can't fake.

I'd tell the **football lads** and other juniors to start learning now.
think: Five years is **enough for me** if I don't bury my head.
By 2034 I want to be good at **what robots do badly**.

Learn **AI tools** slowly, one at a time, from about a year in.
Buy the **second-hand car**, since five years leaves time to earn it back.
feel: **Uneasy**, like an inspection due next year, not next week.
S3.quote: By 2034 I want to be the nurse who's good at the bits robots are bad at.
fieldNote: The extra time lets him **plan instead of brace**.
His spending follows the clock: the **car** comes back with five years' warning.
His grandad's **dementia** steers him toward mental health work.

steps.text: Take a part-time mental health nursing course over two years
Learn one AI tool at a time, starting about a year in

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and most of what people predict ten years out doesn't happen the way they say. At work I'd probably say, wake me up in 2035. Not very helpful, I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine. In ten years I'd be an experienced nurse, maybe a charge nurse, and robots in 2039 would be helping me lift people, not replacing me. I'd still be the one who knows which patient hates his tea strong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, do the wound care course, and maybe the mental health course later. I'd let the AI stuff come to me as the hospital brings it in. I'd buy the car this year and keep saving the rent money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels far away, maybe too far away to worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe too far away to worry about. Is that a problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. I know myself; if AGI is ten years off, I'll do nothing for eight of them. Kerem would have to nag me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the hospital to do with those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Train us properly, in work time, not in a ninety-minute online module at midnight. And keep the ward clerks and assistants in jobs, moving them over to new roles. Barbara deserves better than a computer taking her desk.

say: I'd say **ten-year predictions** rarely happen the way people claim.
I'd joke at work: **wake me up** in 2035.
think: In ten years I'd be an **experienced nurse**, maybe a charge nurse.
Robots in 2039 would **help me lift**, not replace me.
do: Carry on with my shifts and do the **wound care course**.
Buy the **car** this year and keep saving the rent money.
Let **AI tools** come to me as the hospital brings them in.
feel: **Calm**, maybe too calm, because it feels so far away.
S4.quote: If AGI is ten years off, I'll do nothing for eight of them.
fieldNote: He admits he'd **do nothing** for eight years without his brother nagging.
He wants **training in work time**, not midnight online modules.

steps.text: Carry on surgical shifts and complete the wound care course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's the robots in 2031 that land right where I'm weakest, and I'd have no time to catch up. What would help is training in work hours, by a real person, at a normal pace. And honestly, a hospital that keeps a few of us who know how to run a ward when the computers go down.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the old ways. Everybody wants to know who'll learn the new stuff, but somebody has to remember how to run a ward with a pen when the power's out. I'd like that to count for something.

headlineQuote: Somebody has to remember how to run a ward with a pen when the power's out.
portrait: Omar, 27, is a **junior surgical nurse** who writes notes in a paper notebook first.
He has solid savings and co-owns a **rented-out flat** with his brother Kerem.
Pragmatic and dry, he shrugs off slow change because his day is **drains and dressings**.
Fast AGI scares him because **2031 robots** would do the exact tasks he's still learning.
Given time, he'd move toward **mental health nursing**, but admits he might drift.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots arrive by 2031 before he can catch up.
whatWouldHelp: **Training in work hours**, taught by a person at a normal pace.
Hospitals keeping staff who can **run a ward** when computers fail.
